Housing & Homelessness
Control of LA’s federal homeless money is about to change. Here’s what happens next
Nick Gerda
is an accountability reporter who has covered local government in Southern California for more than a decade.
Published November 13, 2026 at 5:19 PM PST
A homeless encampment along the 101 Northbound offramp is seen near City Hall in downtown Los Angeles on Friday, August 21, 2026.
Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
Los Angeles Times)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The nonprofits that run the Los Angeles region's federally funded homeless shelters, outreach teams and housing services will soon be overseen by a different government agency, under a deal a federal judge says he plans to approve next week.
If approved, the shift will mark the biggest change in the control of federal homeless dollars in L.A. in decades.
The proposed settlement would shift federal grants and duties from the troubled L.A. Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) to the county government in stages, starting next month. LAHSA’s management of federal dollars for homeless services would end in June. The deal between LAHSA and the Trump administration keeps the region's request for roughly $240 million in new annual federal funding on track and adds tighter checks on how that money is spent.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said at a Friday hearing he would likely sign it Monday, ending LAHSA's lawsuit over the Trump administration’s June suspension of the agency.
“This has been an absolute past dereliction of duty by the federal government” and local governments, Carter said, referring to what he called decades of failure to properly oversee homelessness dollars.
“I choose now to turn this back to the proper governing bodies,” Carter said. "But please, this can never happen again."
Citing past audits and reports, Carter said “HUD’s been on notice since 2007” of LAHSA’s oversight failures and “abandoned” its own oversight role.
Sponsored message
“I termed it a partnership in failure,” he added. “Local government turned an absolute blind eye to the distribution of these funds and transparency and accountability for these funds.”
“And what is so sad and disappointing is, these funds were meant to serve the absolute most vulnerable in our society,” the judge added.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, left, shown in West L.A. on Wednesday, Aug. 21, 2024.
Brian van der Brug/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
Los Angeles Times)
LAHSA has faced major problems in recent years. Last year, an LAist investigation found the signature of LAHSA’s then-CEO, Va Lecia Adams Kellum, finalized a $2.1 million contract with the nonprofit where her husband was working in senior leadership, despite previously telling LAist she was “completely recused.”
LAist also found the agency kept awarding millions in contract renewals to another nonprofit even after LAHSA’s own compliance team labeled it “high-risk” for, among other things, billing for services while reporting no enrolled participants. That group’s leader, Alex Soofer, recently pleaded guilty to diverting $2 million. Another nonprofit operator contracted with LAHSA, Michael Young, was arrested and charged by federal prosecutors with misappropriating millions of tax dollars, including allegedly siphoning $1 million into a high-end nightclub.
Additionally, a 2024 L.A. County audit found LAHSA had mismanaged hundreds of millions in contracts for homeless services, often paying service providers late and failing to track whether services were provided.
Under the deal, Carter would receive quarterly reports on progress and could intervene if one of the parties asks him to resolve a dispute.
Sponsored message
When control would shift
The deal, on its own, does not change which nonprofits provide shelter, outreach and housing. It instead changes which government agency pays them and ensures they’re serving people as required.
Here’s what the timeline will be if Carter follows through on approving the deal:
Within two weeks of this year's federal awards: Most new grants awarded to LAHSA will instead be managed by the county, not LAHSA.
Starting Dec. 1: Grants for programs that begin on or after that date move to the county before they start.
January 2027: LAHSA, which has overseen the homeless counts since 2005, runs the annual homeless count one last time. The county runs it after that.
By March 1, 2027: The county is approved to take over as the agency that applies for federal homelessness money for the whole region going forward, instead of LAHSA.
By April 1, 2027: The county takes over management from LAHSA of many federal grants for programs already underway that continue past June 2027.
By June 30, 2027: LAHSA finishes administering federal grants that end by this date.
By Dec. 31, 2027: The county takes over the region’s federally required database, known as HMIS, that tracks which homeless services each person receives. The county also takes over another system, known as CES, that matches people with taxpayer-funded housing. With that, LAHSA's last remaining federal roles end.
January 2028: The county conducts the annual homeless count, taking over that role from LAHSA.
What the deal would mean for services
The federal government’s attorneys said the goal is to have stronger oversight over homelessness spending, after many years of documented failures by LAHSA. Attorneys who struck the proposed settlement said in court Friday that the timeline was structured to ensure a smooth transition that doesn’t disrupt homeless services.

Space shuttle Endeavour launches its final chapter at the CA Science Center. How to explore its home
Makenna Cramer
has been covering space shuttle Endeavour's journey at the California Science Center for three years.
Published November 13, 2026 at 10:12 AM PST
Updated November 13, 2026 at 10:46 AM PST
The California Science Center officially opened the space shuttle Endeavour's new permanent home Friday.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
After decades of planning and years of construction, the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is officially open in Exposition Park.
The center is space shuttle Endeavour’s new permanent home and a 200,000-square-foot expansion of the California Science Center. The multi-level galleries feature 100 artifacts and 100 new hands-on exhibits for visitors to explore.
Endeavour is the star of the show in the shuttle gallery, towering 20 stories tall in its vertical launch position. It’s the world’s only display of an authentic space shuttle system, according to museum officials.
Dozens of astronauts attended a ceremony Friday morning under the space shuttle, including the crew of Endeavour's final mission and its commander U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly. Kelly described Endeavour as "the greatest spaceship that ever was."
His colleague, U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, said that having grown up in Pacoima in the San Fernando Valley, he knows what this moment means for thousands upon thousands of children who will be coming through the new center.
"Who will be inspired not just to become future scientists and engineers — I guarantee you some of those young girls and boys will be a future astronaut," Padilla said during the ceremony.
The California Science Center has free general admission. The Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is also free to visit, except for a $4 online reservation service fee for those who aren’t members of the museum.
Sponsored message
Here’s what you need to know.
How do I get there?
The California Science Center is located at 700 Exposition Park Drive. Keep an eye out for the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center’s shiny silver building poking into the sky.
The exterior of the California Science Center and the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
California Science Center)
Parking for cars and school buses is $20 until 5 p.m. and $24 after 5 p.m. Parking for charter buses, limousines, RVs and other larger vehicles is $42.
For public transportation, you can take the Metro E Line to the Expo Park/USC Station.
Sponsored message
You can learn more and find directions here.
How do I get in?
There are timed reservations for the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center because of expected high demand. You can find all the details and learn more here.
You’ll enter through the second floor of the California Science Center, to the right of the escalators if you’re facing forward and across from the Ecosystems exhibit.
There is no time limit once you’re inside. The California Science Center is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, except for Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.
Hundreds of students were the first visitors officially welcomed into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
What do I need to know once I get inside?
Restrooms are on every level of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, and a food court is on the first floor of the California Science Center.
Sponsored message
If you need a baby changing room, it's located in the gender-neutral/family restrooms.
Where can I find merch?
You can exit the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center through a gift shop. There’s also the Explorastore toward the entrance of the building.
California Science Center’s expansion for space shuttle Endeavour to open this fall
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
What are some must-see stops?
It’s tempting to run straight for the space shuttle, but there are tons of other exhibits and artifacts to see along the way.
After taking a glass elevator up the side of the space shuttle, you can look over the gallery and Endeavour from a glass-floor platform.
Mike Kelley
Courtesy ZGF Architects)
Endeavour spans about 20 stories tall.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
Walter Cho, chairman of Korean Air, celebrated the first aircraft installed in the Korean Air Aviation Gallery, including the front of a real Boeing 747-400 that was built for the airline in 1993.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
Three thematic areas in the Kent Kresa Space Gallery include humans in space, robots in space and Rocket Science, according to the museum.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
The trio of galleries span four floors, covering 100,000 square feet of exhibit space, according to the museum.
Makenna Cramer
LAist)
Sponsored message
In the Korean Air Aviation Gallery, you can walk through the front 70 feet of a Boeing 747 where you’ll be able to take a five-minute video “flight” from Los Angeles to Seoul, according to the museum.
In the Kent Kresa Space Gallery, you can program the path of a miniature rover on Mars and build your own robotic spacecraft for a mission. There are also artifacts on display that are on loan from the Smithsonian, including flown capsules from NASA’s Mercury and Gemini projects.
Last but not least, in the Samuel Oschin Shuttle Gallery, lies Endeavour. You can see the space shuttle from multiple levels, including underneath the main engines and from a glass-floor platform that takes you above the entire gallery. There’s also a pair of silver slides that fly down 45 feet to represent the shuttle’s descent and landing.

Published November 13, 2026 at 12:20 PM PST

Officials wind down Lineage warehouse air monitoring
Air quality officials say sensors near the burned-out warehouse in Boyle Heights haven’t picked up anything abnormal since the cleanup finished in September.
Topline:
Air quality officials certified Friday that Lineage has completed all requirements to comply with its order of abatement linked to its burned-out Boyle Heights warehouse and said they’ve ended nearly five months of monitoring.
About the odor complaints: Air quality officials first started citing Lineage due to rotten food smells in mid-July, weeks after the fire that took out the cold storage facility. Over 4,200 complaints were registered at the time, prompting South Coast Air Quality Management District to issue a notice of abatement Aug. 6. Since cleanup finished in early September, the agency said it received two complaints whose sources it could not trace back to the warehouse.
What was being monitored: The South Coast AQMD was testing for ammonia, methane, hydrogen sulfide, particulate matter, air toxic metals and other potentially harmful compounds. The final cleanup of Lineage’s warehouse, completed Sept. 5, was weeks after the deadline given by the city and air quality officials. Lineage has maintained that it conducted the cleanup as quickly and safely as it could.
The backstory: The fire, which started June 17 and burned through Lineage’s cold storage facility, left thousands of tons of rotting food to spoil in the summer heat. For months, people in and near Boyle Heights complained of odors, poor air quality and pests. The fire sparked an outcry among nearby residents in Boyle Heights and East L.A., spurring a new accountability law for cold storage facilities signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September.
What’s next: Lineage could still face fines linked to 39 separate notices of violation that the South Coast AQMD issued between July 12 and August 28. According to the agency, those notices are still working through the enforcement process and could result in fines of up to $75,000 per day per violation. Separately, the state has launched a criminal investigation, and several lawsuits related to the fire are also still playing out. Notably, Lineage sued the company that operated the warehouse’s rooftop solar panels, alleging that faulty electrical connections on the solar array started the fire. (The solar panel operator, Altus Power, has denied the claims.)
Can the warehouse be rebuilt: It’s still an open question, but L.A. city leaders are opposed to Lineage operating there again. Mayor Karen Bass and the L.A. City Council have both taken action to withhold rebuilding permits for the warehouse. Mayor-elect and Councilmember Nithya Raman has also opposed Lineage rebuilding.

Old tech blamed for the ground stop that caused flight chaos: 'It got overloaded'
By Joel Rose, Juliana Kim, Bill Chappell | NPR
Published November 13, 2026 at 8:05 PM PST
Flights listed on a board at an airport.
AP)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Updated November 13, 2026 at 20:38 PM ET
The nationwide ground stop that paralyzed the U.S. aviation system on Friday has ended, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The rare stop, which lasted about four hours, grounded thousands of flights at all U.S. airports in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the September 11th attacks.
In a Friday night news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed outdated technology for the failures.
"We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," he said.
But when pressed by reporters on exactly why those systems would become overwhelmed on an otherwise normal travel day, Duffy did not have a ready answer.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.
Sponsored message
"We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack," he said.
A flight board showing delayed flights is pictured at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Friday.
Tom Brenner
AP)
As of 9 p.m. ET, more than 8,000 flights had been delayed Friday and 7,000 had been canceled in the U.S., according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The turmoil comes on the heels of nearly 7,000 flight delays on Thursday.
The FAA said the issue affected Air Route Traffic Control Centers — the regional air traffic control centers across the country that handle high-altitude traffic.
FAA leaders did not brief the media at the White House press conference, and did not provide any further detail on the communication outages that led to the ground stop.
This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.
That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.
Sponsored message
Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) released a statement late Friday evening calling for a "prompt, penetrating investigation" into the causes of Friday's ground stop.
"A widespread communication outage of this scale is highly alarming — a clear danger to national security, as well as safe, convenient travel close to the holidays. The Department of Transportation owes Americans credible, accurate action and factual disclosure," the statement read.
The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.
"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
Passengers stranded
The nationwide ground stop caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancellations during the holiday season.
At the Friday night press conference, Duffy said flights would resume but would take time to clear.
Sponsored message
At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.
"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said Friday afternoon.
An airline worker shows people how to apply for a refund at LaGuardia airport on Friday.
Adam Gray
Getty Images)
Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she said she was thinking about how soon she could make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.
"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.
At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Giliann Karon was on board a plane when the ground stop was ordered. Karon said she had already experienced a flight delay the day before due to bad weather in New York City, where she is heading.
"It's just kind of like, 'Oh, of course this is happening,'" she said.
Sponsored message
Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

LA needs more childcare options for babies. LAUSD could soon help
Elly Yu
reports on early childhood. From housing to health, she covers issues facing the youngest Angelenos and their families.
Published November 12, 2026 at 5:10 PM PST
The Los Angeles Unified School District is looking to lease spaces in its schools for infant and toddler care.
Photo by Anne Wernikoff
CalMatters)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The Los Angeles Unified School District may lease spaces in its elementary, middle and high schools to use as childcare spaces for babies.
The district is putting together a list of qualified providers and looking to identify spaces it could lease.
Ranae Amezquita, executive director of the district’s early childhood education division, said once the district has a list of spaces, it will start a request for proposal process that childcare providers can apply to during the 2027-2028 school year.
Why is LAUSD looking to expand childcare options now?
In April, LAUSD board members passed a resolution in an aim to expand childcare and early education slots in the district.
The district currently runs about 90 preschools, called early education centers, for children 2 to 4 years old, but it has only four centers that serve children under 2. “The problem with infant care — the reason we can't open them ourself at this time, is because of the cost,” said Amezquita at a board meeting Thursday.
The need for local infant and toddler childcare is high. In 2022, L.A. County assessed that the county only had enough licensed spaces to care for 4% of kids under 2. At the same time, the district has been facing declining enrollment amid lower birth rates. The resolution to expand early childhood care aims to, in part, strengthen the enrollment pipeline into the district.

Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts
By Lauren Sommer | NPR
Published November 13, 2026 at 9:30 AM PST
Coral reefs are highly vulnerable to heat, like these bleached corals in Thailand in 2024. If the planet continues to warm at the current rate, the majority of the world's reefs aren't likely to survive.
Sirachai Arunrugstichai
Getty Images)

Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts
Countries have gathered at the annual climate change negotiations at the COP31 summit in Turkey to discuss how to achieve a goal that is increasingly unachievable. A decade ago, countries agreed to limit climate warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). Now, that goal is out of reach.
Globally, average temperatures are already close to 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were before the Industrial Revolution. Heat-trapping emissions from burning fossil fuels are still rising in the atmosphere, and most countries are not on track to meet their climate pledges to cut emissions by transitioning to cleaner energy.
The best-case scenario for the planet is now 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius of warming (roughly 3 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a recent United Nations study. If fossil fuel emissions stay on their current path, the world would be around 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter by the end of the century.
While the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees Celsius may seem tiny, scientific research shows those increments can produce dramatically different outcomes for the planet. More warming raises the risk of extreme weather globally and could lead to the collapse of some of the planet's most sensitive ecosystems.
Loading...
"The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, climate professor at the University of Exeter. "Every fraction of a degree that we avoid is really able to do a huge amount of limiting harm."
Coral reefs already close to the edge
Corals are architects of an entire ecosystem. As they grow, they create the framework that supports vast numbers of other species, making reefs biodiversity hotspots. They're also vital to hundreds of millions of people who depend on them for food and livelihoods.
Sponsored message
Corals are also highly vulnerable to heat. Prolonged marine heat waves cause corals to bleach, turning them white, which can eventually kill corals. Since the late 1990s, there have been four global bleaching events. With a historically strong El Niño now raising water temperatures, scientists say the fifth global bleaching event is likely unfolding.
Even before the previous bleaching event from 2023 to 2025, researchers found that 44% of coral species globally are at risk of extinction.
"These are incredibly worrying statistics, but they also emphasize that time matters," says David Obura, director of the coral research organization CORDIO East Africa, who worked on the study published last month in the journal Nature. "Every ten years, every five years counts."
Given their susceptibility to heat, the survival of most coral reefs depends on the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees of warming. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found that beyond 2 degrees Celsius of warming, 99% of corals would be lost.
"At 2 degrees of warming, we anticipate most corals just won't survive, not in functional ways to build a reef ecosystem," Obura says. "So you might still find some of the species, but many of them may be so rare or so compromised that they will have gone extinct by then."
With the dire forecasts for the future of coral, conservation groups and coastal communities are working to make reefs as healthy as possible in many areas so they can better withstand climate change. That includes restoring corals, reducing water pollution and even breeding more heat-tolerant corals.
"Most people around the world don't have the luxury of giving up on degraded ecosystems, because that's where they live," Obura says. "That's all they have. So we have to work out how to make them function again."
Sponsored message
Millions more exposed to extreme heat
The goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius is an average temperature, measured across the planet. What it masks is the increasingly extreme heat events that are raising the average.
Researchers have found that for every tenth of a degree of warming, an additional 140 million people are exposed to dangerous levels of heat.
Heat waves are already causing heavy death tolls, like in Europe, where an estimated 50,000 people died of heat-related causes this past summer. Heat is particularly dangerous for those with chronic health conditions, as well as for people who are elderly or pregnant. The real toll of heat waves is often hidden, since many heat-related deaths are undercounted.
"You could think of it a bit like a tipping point for the human organism or body," Lenton says. "At some point, our physiology kind of reaches a tipping point and the worst tipping point is death."
Powerful storms
Every degree of climate change also affects the intensity of storms. Warmer air can produce heavier downpours because it holds 7% more water vapor for every degree. Rainstorms are already getting more intense in most of the U.S.

Scientific research also shows higher levels of warming could lead to other risky tipping points, like the collapse of Antarctic glaciers. If they destabilize, the melt would add vast volumes of water to the ocean, raising sea levels globally.

USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino is leaving for Manchester United
Updated November 13, 2026 at 14:04 PM ET
Mauricio Pochettino, who took over an ailing U.S. men's national soccer team in 2024 and led the squad to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is departing to take over as coach of the famed English Premier League club Manchester United.
Pochettino was the highest-profile manager the U.S. men's team had ever hired. His aggressive attacking style of play won praise from his players and fans alike. At the 2026 World Cup, the USMNT finished first in its group and won its first knockout-round game since 2002. Pochettino's three wins were the most at any World Cup by a USMNT coach.
In a press conference Friday, an emotional Pochettino described the move as "one of the most difficult decisions" of his career. He had been "excited" about the project of revamping the U.S. men's national team, he said, but ultimately the offer from Manchester United represented "the next step to try to make your dreams come true."
U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson credited Pochettino with raising the standard across the federation, and especially the men's program, which has long been viewed as a cut or two below traditional soccer powers in Europe and South America yet has ambitions of competing at the highest levels. "The belief of what's possible for soccer in this country has never been higher," Batson said.
When Pochettino arrived, there were only about 18 months remaining before last summer's World Cup. In that limited time, he set out to tear down what he saw as a culture of complacency and rebuild the roster from the ground up. He evaluated more than 70 players, ultimately uncovering several key contributors to the World Cup roster.
"He's meant so much to me. He's helped me develop as a player and as a person. As a player, that's all you can ask for, to have that trust and that belief in you," said midfielder Sebastian Berhalter.
Sponsored message
As a player, Pochettino represented Argentina in the 2002 World Cup and played in soccer leagues in Spain and France. As a coach, he managed some of Europe's most recognizable clubs: Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain. In August, he signed an extension to lead the USMNT through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full four-year cycle to build the team into a true contender.
Pochettino will lead the U.S. for two more games — both against Haiti in the coming days — before departing for Manchester United.
Steve Cherundolo, the former USMNT player and former head coach of the MLS club LAFC, will take over as interim head coach while U.S. Soccer searches for a permanent replacement for the next cycle leading up to the 2030 World Cup.
"Our ambition is high, and we believe that this is one of the great coaching jobs in the world," Batson said.

Voters reject conservative California school board candidates in several local races
EdSource
Published November 13, 2026 at 3:00 PM PST
Campaign signs for Davis Joint Unified School District school board candidates are displayed outside a home in Davis.
Tanya Perez
EdSource)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Left-leaning candidates running in three school board contests flagged by EdSource as races to watch are each leading comfortably in unofficial election results more than a week after a so-called “blue tsunami” swept the country.
Unofficial results also show progressive candidates ahead in some races in the Inland Empire, a conservative stronghold where several far-right school board candidates ran on issues such as gender identity and parents’ rights. Counties have until Dec. 3 to certify election results.
In the Orange Unified School District, four moderate incumbents are far ahead of conservative challengers in separate races. One of them, board President Stephen Glass, defeated challenger Jack Chang, and has declared victory. The conservative candidates ran largely on parents’ rights and fiscal responsibility.
“We won,” Glass said on social media. “We’ll keep putting students first and supporting every teacher, every classified professional and every family.”
All four incumbents are up by double-digit percentage points, Orange County election results show. The election follows last year’s recall of two conservative school board members.
In a race for the Davis Unified school board, an anti-transgender candidate who once stripped down to a bikini at a school board meeting, lost decisively, according to unofficial election results. Beth Bourne, president of the Yolo County chapter of Moms For Liberty, trails incumbent Elizabeth Moon by 89 percentage points, results show.
In Palo Alto — where issues over academics dominated the race — newcomers Avery Wang and Linda Henigin are ahead in unofficial results for two seats. John Craig, who ran in tandem with Wang, conceded on election night. Wang ran primarily on retaining academic rigor, especially in math. “It’s the beginning of a movement,” Wang told Palo Alto Online.
Sponsored message
Henigin ran on a platform of improving student well-being following a recent spate of student suicides.
Elsewhere in the state, school board candidates in conservative strongholds such as Chino Valley and Temecula fared poorly in local school board races.
In Temecula, school board President Joseph Komrosky trails challenger David Sola by 10 percentage points, results show. Sola has declared victory. Komrosky had voted to ban critical race theory in district schools and attempted to ban teaching materials that mentioned slain gay rights icon Harvey Milk, drawing a sharp rebuke from Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Komrosky’s apparent defeat was part of what The Press-Enterprise reported as “a seismic shift in local governance given recent elections that gave power to the Christian right.”
In Chino Valley Unified in San Bernardino County, two conservative school board candidates are trailing far behind, results show. Chris Shaw, the husband of State Superintendent of Public Instruction candidate Sonja Shaw, trails Frank Gerdine by nearly 17 percentage points, while Meagan Lichthart is ahead of Shaun Smith, backed by Shaw, by 15 percentage points.
